idea: Build the post on one number that runs against what the reader expects.
structure: The number; why it is surprising; where it comes from and how sure it is; what explains it; what follows for the reader.
openingMove: State the number and the expectation it breaks, in two plain sentences.
evidenceType: a measured figure with a known source
fitsWhen: the material holds a real, sourced figure that most readers would guess wrong
pitfalls: a number that is only mildly surprising
a figure whose source cannot be shown
explaining the number away until it is no longer interesting
steal: Lead with the fact the reader would have bet against, then earn it.

idea: Take a common practice apart and show where it fails.
structure: The practice as people do it; why it seems right; the case where it breaks; the cause; what to do instead.
openingMove: Describe the practice fairly, so a reader who follows it nods.
evidenceType: a worked case or a test of the practice
fitsWhen: the writer has seen a widely used method fail in a way that generalises
pitfalls: a straw version of the practice
one failure presented as a law
steal: Steelman the habit first; the break lands harder when the reader agreed with it.

idea: Tell one real case from start to finish and let the lesson come out of it.
structure: The situation; what was tried; what went wrong or right; the moment it turned; what it shows beyond itself.
openingMove: Drop the reader into the situation at the point where something was at stake.
evidenceType: a case the writer knows first-hand
fitsWhen: the material is a single project, incident or decision with a clear arc
pitfalls: detail that does not bear on the lesson
a lesson bolted on at the end
a case too private to be useful to anyone else
steal: Let the case carry the argument; state the lesson once, after the reader has already seen it.

idea: Show the same thing before and after one change, and name the change.
structure: The before, concretely; the change; the after, measured the same way; why the change mattered; when it would not.
openingMove: Show the before as the reader would recognise it in their own work.
evidenceType: two states measured the same way
fitsWhen: the writer made one change and can show its effect
pitfalls: an after measured differently from the before
no word on when the change would not help
steal: Hold everything still but one thing, so the reader can see what moved.

idea: Tell a mistake the writer made and what it taught.
structure: What the writer believed; what they did; how it went wrong; what they understand now; how a reader can avoid it.
openingMove: Admit the mistake in the first lines, plainly, without softening it.
evidenceType: the writer's own experience, with its consequences
fitsWhen: the writer has a real error with a cost and a lesson others can use
pitfalls: a humble-brag dressed as a mistake
a lesson too general to act on
blaming circumstances for the whole of it
steal: Spend the reader's trust on an honest cost, then pay it back with something they can use.

idea: Give the reader a guide to recognise and handle a set of situations.
structure: What the guide covers and for whom; each situation with how to spot it and what to do; the one that matters most; where the guide stops.
openingMove: Name the situation the reader is in when they need this guide.
evidenceType: patterns drawn from repeated experience, each with an example
fitsWhen: the material is a set of related cases the writer has handled many times
pitfalls: a list with no reason it is in that order
steal: Make each entry recognisable in the wild: how to spot it before what to do about it.
